title: Aldinger v. Howard (1976)
summary: The Court refused to use pendent jurisdiction to add the county when the then-governing federal statutory scheme excluded that defendant.
notes:
The book notes later changes concerning municipal liability and Congress’s enactment of § 1367. This is a historical holding, not a freestanding current rule that counties cannot be sued under § 1983.

Aldinger was a clerk in the Spokane County treasurer's office who was fired without a hearing for living with her boyfriend; she sued the treasurer under section 1983 and joined Spokane County on a state-law claim, and the Court (Rehnquist, J.) held that Congress's then-understood exclusion of counties from section 1983 barred pendent-party jurisdiction over the county, a result later addressed by Monell (1978) and by 28 U.S.C. section 1367(a).

sections.Parties: Aldinger asserted a federal civil-rights claim against county officials and sought to add a state-law claim against the county itself.
sections.Material Facts: The state and federal claims were factually connected, but the county was not a proper defendant under the interpretation of § 1983 applicable at the time. The requested expansion would add a party over whom the independent federal claim did not supply jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected the asserted pendent-party jurisdiction. The casebook presents it as part of the historical path to the supplemental-jurisdiction statute.
sections.Issue: Did Gibbs’s factual relationship permit adding a new defendant whom the relevant federal statutory scheme excluded?
sections.Holding: No, in the statutory setting then presented.
sections.Reasoning: The factual overlap did not by itself answer whether Congress had authorized the court to adjudicate the additional party’s liability. The Court considered the structure and implications of the statute supplying original jurisdiction. This made the pendent-party inquiry different from simply adding another claim against a party already properly before the court.

learning.why: The Court refused to use pendent jurisdiction to add the county when the then-governing federal statutory scheme excluded that defendant.

topics.cp-pendent-parties: Adding a new party raised a statutory question beyond the factual relationship of claims.
topics.cp-supplemental-history: The decision belongs to the pre-§ 1367 development and the then-existing treatment of counties under § 1983.
topics.cp-usc-1367: Section 1367(a) later authorized pendent-party jurisdiction, reversing the Aldinger/Finley line for federal-question cases.
topics.cp-federal-question: The anchor claim was a section 1983 federal-question claim against the treasurer, and the holding turned on the scope of that statute.

mnemonic.rationale: A county clerk fired for her living arrangements
